questions.title: What specific factual allegations regarding 'property' must an indictment contain after Ciminelli v. United States?
questions.question_body: I'm reading United States v. Constantinescu and the 5th Circuit is reversing the dismissal, but it hinges on this post-Ciminelli pleading standard. The District Court dismissed because the indictment alleged deprivation of economic *information*, not property. For the government to survive a dismissal for Failure to State an Offense now, what specific facts must they include in paragraph 13 regarding the followers leaving money/property?

questions.title: How does the 'fraudulent-inducement' theory differ from the rejected 'right-to-control' theory in Ciminelli?
questions.question_body: Section III.A of the opinion tries to distinguish Constantinescu from Ciminelli by relying on 'fraudulent-inducement' vs 'right-to-control.' In Ciminelli, the Court rejected 'depriving a victim of potentially valuable economic information' as not being a property interest. If the protection is 'deceiving a victim into handing over money,' does that mean if the victim *accepts* the security (the money), no harm was done? I can't reconcile why the court finds this a valid scheme if the followers are buying the stock, not just declining a future transaction.

questions.title: Does securities fraud require the victim to suffer a net pecuniary loss, according to the Kousisis holding?
questions.question_body: The opinion explicitly cites United States v. Kousisis (2025) to say that defendants need not intend to cause economic *harm* to the victim; intended profit is enough. In this pump-and-dump scheme, the investors bought the stock based on false info. If the stock value partially recovers or the investors aren't forced out, is that still fraud? I'm confused about how 'obtaining money' counts as 'injury' if the victims received a thing of value (the stock) in exchange for their money.

questions.title: How does 18 U.S.C. § 1348 'borrowing concepts' from mail fraud affect the 'property' definition for securities fraud?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that § 1348 'borrows key concepts from the mail and wire fraud statutes' and courts often rely on those cases. Since Ciminelli was a wire fraud case, does this statutory borrowing mean securities fraud has the exact same 'property' elements as wire fraud, or is there a legislative intent that links them differently? Why does the Supreme Court's wire fraud logic apply to this securities statute so directly?

questions.title: Does the reversal of the indictment affect the conspiracy charge under § 1349?
questions.question_body: The court reverses the dismissal of the indictment for 'conspiracy to commit securities fraud, in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1349' in addition to the fraud charges. The reasoning focuses on the 'scheme' and 'intent' elements of the substantive fraud. Does the logic applied to § 1348 (Kousisis/Ciminelli) automatically cure the § 1349 deficiency, or should conspiracy charges be analyzed differently regarding the intent to deprive property?
